title: Giri Leads Firouzja In Final After Heroic Defense, Carlsen Stays Above 2800
summary:
GM Anish Giri leads the Final against GM Alireza Firouzja after winning the first set 11-9 in the Total Chess World Championship on Thursday. The fast classic game was critical, and he managed to defend a lost (but tricky) position to maintain his lead. In Bracket 5, GM Magnus Carlsen put himself in a must-win position against GM Vladislav Artemiev by forfeiting both rapid games. He then won the fast classic game on demand to lead the match and stay above 2800.

The last day is Friday, November 20, starting at 9 a.m. ET / 15:00 CET / 7:30 p.m. IST.

Knockout 1: Giri Leads Final

Knockout 2: Niemann Dominates Fight For 5th

Knockout 3: Martirosyan Upsets Arjun

Knockout 4: So Leads Fight For 13th

Knockout 5: Carlsen Wins Fast Classic On Demand

Knockout 6: Praggnanandhaa Leads

The last two days feature the last two sets of matches, with seven games played each day. After the first set, we have established leaders in every bracket. Keep reading, but you can also check out GM Hikaru Nakamura's recap video below.

Knockout 1: Giri Leads Final

Giri, who considered himself an underdog against both GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave and Firouzja in the faster time controls, has scored well against them in this event. More precisely, he said that they have more consistent results in speed chess. But he's shown that he is just as capable in any given event.

Against Vachier-Lagrave, his wins came in rapid and blitz, and the same happened in his first set against Firouzja. In blitz, he won two games and drew two; in rapid, they traded wins; and he saved the fast classic game to win the set. Those two points he gained in blitz made the difference.

Firouzja with White against Giri. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

The blitz portion convincingly went to Giri, but the real test came in rapid chess. When Firouzja won the first game with White to score four points, he had already taken a one-point lead in the match. In that game, the French number-one seized the opportunity to trade two sets of minor pieces, leaving himself with a slightly better pawn structure and potentially better knight. He found a nice trick involving a pawn sacrifice to win the game.

As he would do again, Giri came clutch when it mattered most. He won the next rapid game to regain the lead, making use of Firouzja's time trouble to put away the game, even if the Frenchman came close to finding a defense.

The move wasn't played, but 38.g5!! would have been a great find, with the idea of 39.Be6! to sacrifice the rook for a mating attack. Giri's win was more prosaic, but every win is worth the same four points.

It all came down to the fast classic encounter where Firouzja, with White in a must-win game, allowed his pawns to be doubled in order to open the g-file. Giri said he underestimated Firouzja's position and felt comfortable, only realizing later, "I'm in trouble and then I think I was lost, but I was trying to put up a fight. I was defending well; practically, it was not easy for him to win, and I'm really happy that I managed to survive. Very lucky."

I'm really happy that I managed to survive. Very lucky.

—Anish Giri

This great fight was our Game of the Day, even if it ended in a draw. GM Dejan Bojkov analyzes it below. (His annotations will be added soon.)

In the match for third place, GM Fabiano Caruana won by the same score 11-9 against Vachier-Lagrave. The American won the first two blitz games and drew all the other games to hold onto the two-point lead.

Vachier-Lagrave vs. Caruana. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

The following game was Caruana's second win in blitz, which came after Vachier-Lagrave declined a repetition of moves with 28...Bd7. The move in itself is fine, but he quickly drifted into "only move territory" and didn't manage to defend with under a minute.

In the fast classic game, Caruana opted for the Open Spanish and, in hindsight, called it a "really good opening choice." With 99 accuracy, he gave Vachier-Lagrave no chances.

On Friday, Firouzja and Vachier-Lagrave will have to win the second set in order to reach armageddon tiebreaks.

Knockout 2: Niemann Dominates Fight For 5th

In the second knockout bracket, GM Hans Niemann dominated the first set against GM Jan-Krzysztof Duda, as did GM Ian Nepomniachtchi against GM Liem Le. Niemann and Nepomniachtchi both went undefeated.

The American won the first three blitz games before making a draw in the fourth. Then, he won the first rapid game and made two subsequent draws to win by a seven-point margin. "Today was totally dominant," he said himself. "I think if I can continue winning like I did yesterday, certainly it will not be a problem."

Today was totally dominant

—Hans Niemann

Niemann against Duda. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

Duda, on the other hand, commented: "Overall, my calculation was completely off today. I just didn't see anything." He has one more day to muster his strength and fight back, as does Le.

Knockout 3: Martirosyan Upsets Arjun

In the third bracket, GM Haik Martirosyan upset super-GM Arjun Erigaisi to lead the match. The Armenian GM lost the first three blitz games before making his first draw in the fourth. But then he took the lead with a rapid win, drew the second rapid game, and won the last game for a nearly 100-point, classically rated upset.

Martirosyan finishes a game against Arjun. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

In the consolation match, GM Richard Rapport managed to defeat GM Jorden van Foreest without needing to show up to the fast classic game. He led by an 11-1 margin, so the forfeit of eight points makes the final score, 11-9, look closer than it really was.

Knockout 4: So Leads Fight For 13th

GM Wesley So won the first set against his national teammate GM Levon Aronian. After a quick Berlin draw in the fast classic game, he said, "I think we want to make this primarily a blitz and a rapid match, more than a classical match," while Aronian commented, "I think I'm just too tired."

So leads the fourth bracket. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

Knockout 5: Carlsen Wins Fast Classic On Demand

Carlsen's 2800 rating and world number-one spot were legitimately at risk on Thursday. A draw against Artemiev in the fast classic game would have caused his rating to drop to 2799, the first time he would have dropped under 2800 in 17 years. And if he lost and Caruana won, only in this scenario would Caruana become world number-one.

If you read the headline and first paragraph, you already know what happened. None of the above.

Carlsen wins on demand. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

We can start from the beginning. Carlsen lost the first blitz game but then came back and won the next three. He then told Norwegian TV 2 that he would only return for the fast classical game. Artemiev won both rapid games by forfeit and took the lead, putting Carlsen in a must-win situation. It can be said that Carlsen was in a must-win mindset anyway.

Magnus Carlsen said in an interview that he will not play the two rapid games against Vladislav Artemiev. That means he'll be in a must-win game in the fast classic encounter. In addition to losing the set, a draw would mean Carlsen drops under 2800 for the first time in 17 years. #TotalChess

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 19, 2026

Carlsen said afterward that he wasn't at all confident going into the game. "I hadn't won a game of classical chess the whole tournament and he's very solid," he said. Artemiev, on the other hand, took the loss well.

Honestly, I am very glad this playing day is finished because he was very tough. Every game I have a lot of troubles, no positive moments, and my opponent was much better than me... it's a logical result. Unfortunately, no chance today.

It's a logical result. Unfortunately, no chance today.

—Vladislav Artemiev

Artemiev held his own in the Ruy Lopez, but by move 21 he was in severe time trouble. With one minute against 26 minutes. Carlsen applied pressure, and Artemiev, who defended quite well on the increment, sacrificed a pawn but eventually collapsed—even if the sacrifice was initially sound.

With a 2804 live rating, Carlsen can afford to draw the fast classic game and stay above 2800.

Knockout 6: Praggnanandhaa Leads

GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu leads the Final in the last bracket against GM Abhimanyu Mishra.

Praggnanandhaa wins the first set. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

Friday is the last day, and you won't want to miss it!

How to watch?

You can watch the event on the Chess24 Twitch or YouTube pages, or on GM Hikaru Nakamura's Kick channel. You can find the games on our dedicated events page.

The live broadcast was hosted by GM David Howell, IMs Jovanka Houska and Anna Rudolf, and WIM Fiona Steil-Antoni.

The Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot 2026 takes place on November 10-20 at the Anantara New York Palace Hotel in Budapest, Hungary. The event is a trial run for the official event in 2027, which will crown the first FIDE World Combined Champion. The event consists of a round-robin group stage and a knockout combining blitz, rapid, and fast classical time controls. The time control is 3+2 for blitz, 15+10 for rapid, 45+30 for fast classical, and 10 minutes (White) vs. 7 minutes (Black) with a one-second increment starting on move 41 in armageddon.

additionalSources.title: Total Chess: Giri takes early lead over Firouzja, Carlsen forfeits rapid games
additionalSources.summary:
Anish Giri won the opening set of the Total Chess Pilot final against Alireza Firouzja in Budapest, while Fabiano Caruana did likewise against Maxime Vachier-Lagrave in the match for third place - both sets finished 11–9. Meanwhile, Magnus Carlsen sparked further controversy by forfeiting both rapid games against Vladislav Artemiev before returning to win the fast classic encounter. | Photo: Michal Walusza / Total Chess

Advantage Giri

The Total Chess Pilot has entered its final stretch, with players competing in two-day matches on Thursday and Friday to determine the final standings.

Alireza Firouzja and Anish Giri, who reached the title match after defeating Fabiano Caruana and Maxime Vachier-Lagrave respectively , began their final with a closely contested set. Giri prevailed by an 11–9 score, while Caruana obtained an identical result against MVL in the match for third place. Elsewhere, Magnus Carlsen once again attracted attention by forfeiting games, this time skipping both rapid encounters against Vladislav Artemiev before returning to win the fast classic game (and the set).

The finalists getting ready for a demanding, two-day battle | Photo: Michal Walusza

Anish Giri took the first step towards overall victory in Budapest by defeating Alireza Firouzja 11–9 in Thursday's opening set. The Dutchman gained a 2-point advantage in the blitz section, winning twice, once with each colour, while the remaining two games ended in draws.

The finalists then exchanged victories with the white pieces in the rapid section, leaving Giri with his 2-point lead intact heading into the fast classic encounter, worth 8 points for a win. Playing black, the Dutch number one found himself in a clearly inferior position, but eventually managed to escape with a draw.

Firouzja's crucial mistake was offering a queen trade, which allowed Giri to simplify into an endgame featuring a knight and four pawns against a rook and a single pawn. Giri continued to defend accurately and eventually secured the all-important draw, giving him an 11–9 victory in the first set.

In good spirits - Alireza Firouzja and Anish Giri | Photo: Michal Walusza

The match for third place followed a remarkably similar pattern. Fabiano Caruana defeated Maxime Vachier-Lagrave by the same 11–9 score, also gaining a 2-point advantage in the blitz section thanks to victories with both white and black. The remaining two blitz games ended drawn, as did both rapid encounters and the final fast classic game.

Notably, both Giri and Caruana won their opening sets on the day they had the black pieces in the 8-point fast classic encounter. This means that, should either player find himself in a must-win situation in Friday's final game, he will have the white pieces at his disposal.

Fabiano Caruana got the better of Maxime Vachier-Lagrave | Photo: Michal Walusza

Fifth place and beyond: Niemann continues strong run

In the knockout for fifth place, Hans Niemann continued his good form in Budapest with a 13½–6½ victory over Jan-Krzysztof Duda. The American won three of the four blitz games and one rapid encounter, drawing the remaining games to finish the day unbeaten.

Niemann has already returned to the 2700 club in the live classical ratings thanks to his fast classic results. His performances in Budapest have also helped him climb five places in the rapid live rankings and three places in the blitz rankings.

Meanwhile, Ian Nepomniachtchi obtained a 14–6 victory over Le Quang Liem in the opening set of their match for seventh place. The two players were tied on six points heading into the fast classic encounter, but the Russian grandmaster won the final game convincingly in 44 moves to take the lead.

Hans Niemann won the first set in his match for fifth place against Jan-Krzysztof Duda | Photo: Michal Walusza

A sharp-looking Ian Nepomniachtchi defeated Le Quang Liem | Photo: Michal Walusza

The remaining matches produced the following results:

Ninth place: Haik Martirosyan defeated Arjun Erigaisi, continuing his impressive run against some of the world's leading players.

Eleventh place: Richard Rapport beat Jorden van Foreest 11–9. The Hungarian forfeited the fast classic encounter for the second consecutive day, although this time he had already secured victory in the set. On Wednesday, he had an unsurmountable point deficit in the match when he decided not to play.

Thirteenth place: Wesley So obtained a 7½–5½ first-set victory over Levon Aronian.

Fifteenth place: Vincent Keymer defeated Shakhriyar Mamedyarov 14½–5½, with a victory in the fast classic encounter making the difference.

Seventeenth place: Magnus Carlsen beat Vladislav Artemiev 11–9 despite forfeiting both rapid games, as he went on to win the fast classic encounter.

Nineteenth place: Andrew Hong defeated Bibisara Assaubayeva 15–5, scoring a victory with the white pieces in the fast classic game.

Twenty-first place: Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu prevailed 12–8 over Abhimanyu Mishra in a hard-fought opening set.

Twenty-third place: Nodirbek Abdusattorov obtained a 16–4 victory over Vaishali Rameshbabu.

Vladislav Artemiev | Photo: Michal Walusza

Carlsen forfeits two rapid games, then returns to win

The discussion surrounding forfeited games continued on Thursday, with Magnus Carlsen taking his approach a step further. After declining to play the final fast classic games against Bibisara Assaubayeva on Tuesday and Wednesday, the Norwegian decided to skip both rapid encounters against Vladislav Artemiev, despite their match still being undecided.

Carlsen had started the day by winning three of the four blitz games against Artemiev, losing the remaining encounter after blundering into checkmate in an endgame.

With a 3–1 lead on the scoreboard, he spoke to Norway's TV 2 and announced that he would not return for the rapid section.

I'm not coming back until the fast classic. I think it's fun to play the blitz, but for the rapid, give or take, I would rather be more rested for the classical. If I have drawing odds or not, I could not care less.

Carlsen followed through on his announcement, forfeiting both rapid games and conceding 8 points. He therefore entered the fast classic encounter trailing by 6 points, but still had the opportunity to win the set outright with a victory in the final game.

That is precisely what happened. The Norwegian won the fast classic game to secure an 11–9 victory, while also gaining 2.8 classical rating points. His live rating now stands at 2804.0 , keeping intact his 17-year streak of remaining above the 2800 mark.

It was also Carlsen's first fast classic victory of the tournament. He had gone through the entire ten-game group stage without a win, recording nine draws and one loss, before forfeiting both fast classic encounters against Assaubayeva.

Magnus Carlsen | Photo: Michal Walusza

While some observers considered Carlsen's earlier decisions to skip games in already decided matches understandable, particularly given the fatigue caused by the demanding schedule, his choice to forfeit two games in the middle of an undecided set proved more difficult to justify.

Fabiano Caruana was openly critical of the Norwegian's approach:

I don't think it's good at all. I don't think it was good the first time, but this is even worse because you are leaving in the middle of the match. I think you should just forfeit the match if you don't play.

Anish Giri had already commented on the subject , before Carlsen's latest forfeits, making it clear that he would not consider following the Norwegian's example:

One thing for sure, I wouldn't dare to do it myself, even after what Magnus did - I'm too old for these shenanigans.

Hikaru Nakamura had also expressed his disagreement following Carlsen's earlier forfeits against Assaubayeva. The famed streamer and elite grandmaster argued that any objections to a tournament's regulations should be raised before the competition begins, rather than during the event itself:

As somebody who has played professional chess for a very, very long time, if you have an issue with various things, you bring these issues up before the event. You do not suddenly start creating rules or coming up with scenarios during the event. It’s just unacceptable behavior from Magnus. I feel really bad for Bibisara in this case because she was probably really looking forward to the game.

additionalSources.title: Giri takes the lead in Total Chess Final
additionalSources.summary: Caruana leads the match for third place as Carlsen turns his day around in Fast Classic Anish Giri won the opening day of the final of the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot in Budapest on Thursday, defeating Alireza Firouzja by 11 points to 9. Giri’s advantage in blitz proved decisive after the players exchanged rapid victories and drew their Fast Classic game. A win or draw on Friday would secure Giri the Budapest pilot title without a tiebreak. The scores reset overnight, so Firouzja must win the second day to force an Armageddon tiebreak. Each knockout day has seven games: four Blitz games, two Rapid games and one Fast Classic. A Blitz win is worth one point, a Rapid win four, and a Fast Classic win eight, with half for a draw. Winning both days, or winning one and drawing the other, decides the match. One win apiece, or two drawn days, leads to Armageddon. Fabiano Caruana also took an 11–9 first-day lead against Maxime Vachier-Lagrave in the match for third place. All 24 players were in action as the finals and placement matches began across the six knockout brackets. Giri answers Firouzja’s rapid victory Giri drew the opening blitz game before winning the second with White and the third with Black, the latter after a long battle. A draw in the fourth gave him a 3–1 lead. Firouzja responded by winning the first rapid game with White. However, Giri immediately struck back with a White victory in the second rapid game to regain the lead at 7–5. Four points apiece from the Fast Classic draw preserved Giri’s advantage and completed his third successive daily victory in the knockout stage, following his two wins against Vachier-Lagrave in the semifinals. Caruana moves ahead in the match for third place Caruana won the first two blitz games against Vachier-Lagrave before the remaining five games were drawn. His 3–1 advantage from blitz therefore carried through to an 11–9 daily victory. Caruana needs a win or a tie on Friday to finish third. Vachier-Lagrave must win the second day to take their match to Armageddon. Every player still in action Magnus Carlsen recorded his first Fast Classic win of the event, beating Vladislav Artemiev with White to turn a 3–9 deficit into an 11–9 daily victory in the match for 17th place. Carlsen had won three of the four blitz games, but forfeited both rapid games, meaning he needed the eight-point Fast Classic win to take the day. Hans Moke Niemann remained unbeaten across all seven games against Jan-Krzysztof Duda in the match for fifth place. He won the first three blitz games and the first rapid game, drawing the others to take the day 13.5–6.5. Wesley So also moved ahead, beating Levon Aronian 12.5–7.5 in their match for 13th place. Home favourite Richard Rapport had already secured the day against Jorden van Foreest by taking an 11–1 lead from blitz and rapid. Having already secured the day’s victory, Rapport forfeited the Fast Classic game, resulting in an 11–9 daily victory in their match for 11th place. Day one in the other brackets: Places 5 to 8: Hans Moke Niemann 13.5–6.5 Jan-Krzysztof Duda; Ian Nepomniachtchi 14–6 Liem Le. Places 9 to 12: Haik Martirosyan 14.5–5.5 Arjun Erigaisi; Richard Rapport 11–9 Jorden van Foreest. Places 13 to 16: Wesley So 12.5–7.5 Levon Aronian; Vincent Keymer 14.5–5.5 Shakhriyar Mamedyarov. Places 17 to 20: Magnus Carlsen 11–9 Vladislav Artemiev; Andrew Hong 15–5 Bibisara Assaubayeva. Places 21 to 24: Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu 12–8 Abhimanyu Mishra; Nodirbek Abdusattorov 16–4 Vaishali Rameshbabu. Among the Indian players, Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu took the opening day against Abhimanyu Mishra in their match for 21st place. The blitz games were split 2–2, before Praggnanandhaa won the first rapid game and drew the remaining rapid and Fast Classic games to finish 12–8 ahead. Arjun Erigaisi made a strong start against Haik Martirosyan, winning the first three blitz games and drawing the fourth. Martirosyan recovered from the 0.5–3.5 deficit with a win and a draw in rapid, then won Fast Classic with Black to take the day 14.5–5.5 in the match for ninth place. Vaishali Rameshbabu lost 16–4 to Nodirbek Abdusattorov on the opening day of their match for 23rd place. Developed by Norway Chess and approved by FIDE, the Total Chess World Championship Tour introduces a unified format that crowns the world’s ultimate champion by testing excellence across three disciplines: Fast Classical, Rapid and Blitz. The Tour will bring together the world’s top 24 men and women players to compete across four premier international events hosted in leading global cities. Designed to elevate the sport’s commercial appeal and fan engagement, Total Chess combines world-class competition with innovation, technology and immersive spectator experiences to create a new benchmark for professional chess. With a vision to make chess one of the world’s most engaging and commercially sustainable sports, Total Chess aims to expand the game’s global footprint, inspire the next generation of players, and connect millions of fans through a dynamic championship that celebrates intelligence, strategy and sporting excellence.

title: The difficult road to defending his title: Gukesh Dommaraju
summary:
On 24 November, the first game of the eagerly anticipated World Championship match between defending champion Gukesh Dommaraju and challenger Javokhir Sindarov will be played in Geneva. Never before have two such young players competed for the title. In this article, we introduce the defending champion and offer insights into his career to date. | Photos: ChessBase India, Amruta Mokal / Michal Walusza / Eng Chin An (cover photo) / Tushar Damor /Frederic Friedel

It was a magical moment in chess history when, on 12 December 2024, the final game of the World Chess Championship match approached its dramatic conclusion: Ding Liren had moved his rook to f2 on move 55. It was not a good decision. The move cost him the chance of a tiebreak and, ultimately, lost him his world championship title. On the other side of the board, just a few moves later, a relieved, exhausted and understandably stunned Gukesh Dommaraju broke down in tears.

At the age of 18 years and 197 days, Gukesh claimed the chess crown as the youngest and 18th world champion in chess history!

Gukesh with his World Championship trophy. | Photo: Eng Chin An

Many experts and fans had predicted a much more convincing victory for the Indian, as he was facing a Ding Liren who had been struggling psychologically since winning the title in April 2023. How history can repeat itself ...

Who is this young Indian?

Gukesh Dommaraju – Profile

Born: 29 May 2006

Place of birth: Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India

GM 2019, IM 2018, FM 2015

World champion: since 12 December 2024

Youngest world chess champion in history

Gukesh was born on 29 May 2006 to microbiologist Padmakumari and ear, nose and throat specialist Rajinikanth. At around the age of five, he had his first encounters with the royal game, both within his family, where chess was occasionally played, and at school. These encounters would prove to be momentous.

His exceptional talent soon attracted attention. The first to recognise his ability was Bhaskar V, the chess coach at his school, who noticed Gukesh's extraordinary powers of comprehension. He approached the boy's parents, who increasingly made the development of their talented son's chess skills the focus of their lives. Gukesh was still attending Velammal Vidyalaya School in Chennai, but gradually reduced his attendance. His father even gave up his professional career to support his son at the various stages of his chess career.

Young Gukesh already needs strong neck muscles ... | Photo: ChessBase India

His training schedule was gradually intensified. What had initially been school chess soon developed into systematic instruction. However, Gukesh had to contend with one problem in his early years: his father recalls that, as a child, Gukesh was sometimes "very upset" after defeats.

In 2017, when Gukesh was eleven years old, Indian grandmaster Vishnu Prasanna introduced a more systematic approach to the young player's training. He became an important mentor, placing particular emphasis on independent thinking without engines. Among other things, he also focused on his pupil's strategic and mental development, appreciating his great work ethic and exceptional talent.

Sagar Shah and Gukesh analysing together. | Photo: Amruta Mokal

Later, Polish GM Grzegorz Gajewski also joined Team Gukesh. He would play a special role in the further development of Gukesh's opening repertoire and in his World Championship preparation – but there was still a long way to go before then ...

The list of other coaches reads like a who's who of chess: Sandipan Chanda, Artur Jussupow, Boris Gelfand and, of course, Viswanathan Anand, the former world champion whose successes had initiated the rise of Indian chess.

First international successes

Winner of the U9 category at the Asian Schools Chess Championships

FIDE Master in 2015

U12 World Champion in 2018

Five gold medals at the Asian Youth Chess Championships (individual classical chess, as well as individual and team events in blitz and rapid chess)

International Master in 2018

Stepping into the spotlight

At the age of just twelve years, seven months and 17 days, Gukesh earned his grandmaster title. The date was 15 January 2019. Following his success at the 17th Delhi International Grandmaster Open , he was, at that time, the second-youngest grandmaster in chess history. Only Sergey Karjakin had achieved the title at a younger age.

Meeting Frederic Friedel

Frederic Friedel, one of the founders of ChessBase, met Gukesh personally during his rapid rise. In January 2019, Friedel attended a tournament in Mumbai. Sagar Shah, the head of ChessBase India, introduced him to twelve-year-old Gukesh. "I was surprised to learn that the boy had already achieved two GM norms," Friedel recalls. Shortly afterwards, Friedel visited Gukesh at his home in Chennai and learned that he had meanwhile achieved his third GM norm – the "boy" was already a grandmaster!

ChessBase co-founder Frederic Friedel meets Gukesh for the first time on 7 January 2019. | Photo: Frederic Friedel Archive

Frederic Friedel visiting Gukesh and his parents. | Photo: ChessBase India

Friedel, who recognised the potential of the young GM, and that of other young Indian talents, put his network to use: his friend Vladimir Kramnik had just retired from competitive chess. Friedel suggested that the former world champion could train young Indian top talents. After Kramnik agreed, Sagar Shah, with financial support from the company Microsense, organised training camps in France and in Chennai , where former World Championship runner-up Boris Gelfand also joined them. Gukesh, Praggnanandhaa and Arjun Erigaisi were among the young talents – no further words are necessary ...

A return visit to Hamburg in 2025. | Photo: Frederic Friedel Archive

The young grandmaster continues to develop

With the GM title, Gukesh had reached an important milestone, but he was still far from the world's elite. His development took place at a time when India was producing more and more young grandmasters. In addition to those already mentioned, Nihal Sarin and Leon Luke Mendonca should also be named to illustrate the rise of India as a chess nation.

In 2020, however, the coronavirus pandemic abruptly interrupted the normal international tournament circuit. Gukesh used the time to develop his chess skills further and, of course, also competed in online events. In 2021, he finished third behind Praggnanandhaa and Abdusattorov in the Julius Baer Challengers Chess Tour , scoring 14 points from 19 games. An important success for him. But his breakthrough at senior level would come the following year. At the Chess Olympiad in Chennai, Gukesh played on board one for India's second team. He scored a remarkable nine points from eleven games, winning the gold medal on board one. The team claimed bronze – curiously, one place ahead of India 1.

Gukesh had caused a sensation – among other things, he defeated Fabiano Caruana – and demonstrated that he could already hold his own against the very best players in the world.

Further milestones followed:

Crossing the 2700 Elo mark in 2022 as the third-youngest player ever to do so, after Wei Yi and Alireza Firouzja

2023: Gukesh overtakes Viswanathan Anand in the world rankings and crosses the 2750 Elo mark. Anand had previously been India's highest-rated player for 37 years!

In September 2023, he reached eighth place in the world rankings

Gukesh finished second in the 2023 FIDE Circuit and qualified for the 2024 Candidates Tournament because the winner, Caruana, had already qualified through the 2023 World Cup

Sensational victory at the Candidates Tournament in Toronto , where he was the youngest participant at 17, finishing ahead of Caruana and Nepomniachtchi

A few months after the Candidates Tournament, Gukesh played on board one for the Indian team at the Chess Olympiad in Budapest . India won the gold medal for the first time in its history, and Gukesh scored nine points from ten games (a tournament performance rating of 3056 Elo!), earning him another individual board gold medal

Gukesh becomes world number five

World Championship match against Ding Liren

The World Championship match between Gukesh and Ding Liren was extremely exciting and almost went to a tiebreak. | Photo: Eng Chin An

The World Championship took place in Singapore from 25 November to 12 December 2024. The situation going into the match seemed clear: challenger Gukesh was in top form, while defending champion Ding Liren appeared to be struggling psychologically with the burden of the world championship title. Many experts even expected a very convincing victory for the challenger. But the match turned out to be extremely tense. As mentioned above, it was only decided in the final classical game, when some were already thinking about the tiebreaks scheduled for the following day. The 18th world champion was just 18 years old, making him the youngest titleholder in World Championship history. He broke the record held by Garry Kasparov, who had been four years and 13 days older when he took the title from Anatoly Karpov after a long battle.

Life as world champion

After his historic World Championship triumph, a new chapter began for Gukesh: from then on, he was no longer the challenger but the defending champion.

Tournament results since winning the title

Tata Steel Masters 2025 in Wijk aan Zee: After losing the tiebreak against Praggnanandhaa, Gukesh finishes second at the traditional Dutch tournament

Norway Chess 2025 : Gukesh remains among the leaders and eventually finishes third behind Carlsen and Caruana

European Club Cup 2025 : Gukesh wins with SuperChess from Romania. On board one, he wins the gold medal with a performance rating of 2927 Elo.

World Cup 2025 in Goa : Gukesh is eliminated as early as the third round by Frederik Svane

World Rapid and Blitz Championships 2025: Gukesh fails to qualify for the final stage

Tata Steel Masters 2026 : Gukesh finishes joint eighth with 6½ points from 13 games

Prague International Chess Festival 2026 : Ninth place out of ten participants with 3½ points from nine games

Norway Chess 2026 : Last place among six players

Chennai Grand Masters 2026 : Gukesh finishes last among eight players with two points from seven games

In 2026, Gukesh decides not to participate in several classical events of the Grand Chess Tour

46th Chess Olympiad 2026 in Samarkand : This time, Gukesh plays on board four for the Indian team and wins the individual board gold medal. In the first ten rounds, he scores seven wins and three draws. His performance rating is 2797 Elo. In the final round, he loses to Hungary's Gleb Dudin.

Norway Chess 2026 was not a good tournament for either the former world champion or the reigning world champion. | Photo: Michal Walusza

A sight that became more common in 2026: a thoughtful and disappointed world champion. | Photo: Tushar Damor

In an interview with the Indian Express, Gukesh's coach Grzegorz Gajewski said that Gukesh's play at the Olympiad had been good, but not outstanding: "Mental stability was particularly important. The results gave Gukesh back his confidence."

In a conversation with the British Chess Magazine, Gukesh himself explained that he had consciously addressed his mental health and that regular meditation had made a difference.

It will therefore certainly be interesting to follow not only the moves on the board during the World Championship match, but also the psychological aspects. It is particularly interesting to observe how the two most recent world champions, Ding Liren and Gukesh Dommaraju, apparently struggled, or are still struggling, considerably with the pressure of holding the world championship title.

title: World Junior U20 Chess Championship 2026 begins in Caracas, Venezuela
summary: Caracas, Venezuela – November 18, 2026. The President of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, Delcy Rodríguez, and the President of the National Assembly, Jorge Rodríguez, made the ceremonial first move to officially launch the 2026 World Junior Chess Championship (U20 category) in Caracas. The event, organized by the Venezuelan Chess Federation with the support of the Ministry of People’s Power for Sports and under the auspices of the International Chess Federation (FIDE), takes place from November 18 to 27 at the Hotel Eurobuilding. The championship features 136 players from 32 countries competing in the Open and Girls categories (11-round Swiss tournaments with classical time controls). Accompanied by FIDE President Timur Turlov, the Minister of People’s Power for Sports Franklin Cardillo, and the President of the Venezuelan Chess Federation Hugo Martínez, the head of state highlighted the significance of hosting a World Championship for this intellectual sport, asserting that the discipline strengthens the cognitive capabilities of young people. “We welcome participants from 32 nations across our continent, as well as from Europe, Asia, and Africa, to our country. This championship provides opportunities for the youth of Venezuela to develop their intellect. At the same time, this sport fosters social interaction and healthy recreation, while instilling discipline. I therefore call for its widespread promotion, so that we may continue to welcome international events of this nature,” she stated. The nations represented at this competition include Germany, Argentina, Aruba, Azerbaijan, Belgium, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Canada, China, Colombia, Costa Rica, Cuba, Curaçao, Ecuador, the United States, India, Kazakhstan, Honduras, Lithuania, Mexico, Nicaragua, Nigeria, Peru, Paraguay, Panama, Puerto Rico, Russia, Suriname, Trinidad and Tobago, Uruguay, and Venezuela. Earlier that day, the Minister of People’s Power for Sports, Franklin Cardillo, welcomed FIDE President Timur Turlov to his office upon his arrival in Venezuela for the grand opening ceremony of the 2026 World Junior Chess Championship (U20) in Caracas. The meeting was also attended by the President of the Venezuelan Olympic Committee, María Soto, and the President of the Venezuelan Chess Federation, Hugo Martínez. They discussed the growing momentum behind the “sport of the mind” and explored strategic alliances to further establish Venezuela as a potential hub for major chess events. Official opening The opening ceremony for the championship took place at the theater in La Carlota. The event was attended by FIDE President Timur Turlov and Venezuelan Chess Federation President Hugo Martínez, alongside athletes, coaches, International Masters, Grandmasters, arbiters, and representatives from the diplomatic corps of several nations accredited to Venezuela. Those in attendance enjoyed a masterful musical performance by the Juan Bautista Plaza Regional Orchestra, part of the “El Sistema” program, featuring pieces that celebrated the vibrant spirit of Venezuela. The ceremony concluded on a festive note with the appearance of “Maya Chess,” the official mascot of the 2026 World Junior Chess Championship.
